[{"name":"ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5 — documented information (controlled-document regime)","tradition":"ISO quality management (ISO/TC 176)","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO 9001:2015, Quality management systems — Requirements, clause 7.5 (iso.org/standard/62085.html). Official public companion: ISO/TC 176/SC2/N1286, Guidance on the requirements for Documented Information of ISO 9001:2015 (iso.org/iso/documented_information.pdf). Clause detail cross-verified via N1286 and consistent secondary sources; the standard text itself is paywalled.","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/62085.html","what_it_defines":"The requirements regime for controlled documents. 7.5.1: the QMS includes documented information required by the standard PLUS whatever the organization determines necessary for effectiveness (extent proportional to organization size, process complexity, competence). 7.5.2 (creating and updating): ensure (a) identification and description (e.g. title, date, author, reference number), (b) format (e.g. language, software version, graphics) and media (paper, electronic), (c) review and approval for suitability and adequacy. 7.5.3 (control): information must be available and suitable for use where and when needed, and adequately protected (loss of confidentiality, improper use, loss of integrity); control activities as applicable: distribution/access/retrieval/use; storage and preservation including legibility; control of changes (e.g. version control); retention and disposition. Documented information of external origin determined necessary must be identified and controlled; information retained as evidence of conformity must be protected from unintended alteration. The 2015 edition merged 'documents' and 'records' into one concept, 'documented information', with two verbs carrying the old distinction: MAINTAIN (keep current — definitional documents) vs RETAIN (keep as evidence — records).","form_elements":["Two-tier scope rule: standard-required information + organization-determined-necessary information, extent proportional to complexity","Creation/update triple: identification-and-description, format-and-media, review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy","Availability rule: relevant version available at point of use, when needed","Obsolete-document rule: prevent unintended use of superseded versions","Change control: changes identified, current revision status known (version control named explicitly)","Control-activity checklist: distribution, access (view-only vs view-and-change), retrieval and use, storage and preservation, retention and disposition","External-origin documents identified and brought under control","Evidence records protected from unintended alteration","maintain (keep current) vs retain (keep as evidence) verb distinction"],"fit_notes":"Direct model for governing versioned prompt/skill/definition surfaces. The mapping is one-to-one: the definition corpus is 'documented information determined necessary'; ratification = review-and-approval for suitability and adequacy; the compiled-context assembly guarantee = relevant-version-available-at-point-of-use; the stale-compiled-prompt hazard = the obsolete-document rule; git + pinning (report §2.7, Langfuse algebra) = change control and revision status; canonical templates from shopsystem-templates = external-origin control; protection-from-unintended-alteration = the immutability rule for ADRs/session records. What ISO adds over what the report already has is the requirements CHECKLIST form — clause 7.5 is itself a derivable audit rubric for the governance layer, and audit traceability (which version was in force when a given artifact was produced) is exactly the judge-model/prompt-version pinning requirement of §2.6/§3. ADAPT: take the requirement checklist and the maintain/retain distinction; drop certification machinery, and let git supply the mechanics ISO leaves to procedure.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"ISO 9000:2015 vocabulary (documented information, record, verification/validation term system)","tradition":"ISO quality management (ISO/TC 176)","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO 9000:2015, Quality management systems — Fundamentals and vocabulary, 4th ed., September 2015, clause 3 (iso.org/standard/45481.html; full text publicly readable on the ISO Online Browsing Platform). Term numbers 3.8.5/3.8.6/3.8.10 verified this session; other terms cited by name.","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/45481.html","what_it_defines":"The controlled term system beneath document control and checking: document = 'information and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.5); documented information = 'information required to be controlled and maintained by an organization and the medium on which it is contained' (3.8.6); record = 'document stating results achieved or providing evidence of activities performed' (3.8.10); specification = a document stating requirements; plus the linked cluster: requirement (need or expectation that is stated, generally implied or obligatory), conformity/nonconformity (fulfilment / non-fulfilment of a requirement), objective evidence, verification (confirmation via objective evidence that SPECIFIED REQUIREMENTS are fulfilled) vs validation (confirmation via objective evidence that requirements for a SPECIFIC INTENDED USE are fulfilled). Definitions are themselves written in a controlled defined-term-references-defined-term style.","form_elements":["document / documented information / record as distinct defined terms","record defined by function: states results achieved or evidences activities performed","specification = document stating requirements","conformity = fulfilment of a requirement (the semantic of every check verdict)","verification vs validation split: against stated requirements vs against intended use","objective evidence as the admissibility condition for both","vocabulary itself maintained as a controlled, cross-referenced term system"],"fit_notes":"ADOPT as citable vocabulary anchors. Three distinctions do real work for the shop: (1) maintained-definition vs retained-record formalizes the split the report already draws in §2.4 (principles amended under change control vs ADRs immutable and superseded) and generalizes it to every artifact kind; (2) verification vs validation maps precisely onto mechanical-checks-against-the-definition vs fitness-judgment-against-intended-use (the §2.6 judged fitness tests are validation, the derived lint/schema checks are verification — naming this prevents category errors in check design); (3) conformity-as-fulfilment-of-a-requirement plus the objective-evidence condition restates the report's Deming operational-definition rule (§2.5a) in standards language. Costs nothing to adopt; the terms are stable, public, and already implicit in the system.","adopt_potential":"adopt"},{"name":"ISO 10013:2021 — Guidance for documented information","tradition":"ISO quality management (ISO/TC 176/SC 3)","source_type":"standard","citation":"ISO 10013:2021, Quality management systems — Guidance for documented information, 1st ed., March 2021, 14 pp. (iso.org/standard/75736.html; replaces ISO/TR 10013:2001). Existence, edition, committee, and scope verified; full text paywalled.","url":"https://www.iso.org/standard/75736.html","what_it_defines":"The how-to companion to 9001 clause 7.5: guidance on developing and maintaining the documented information a QMS needs, tailored to the organization — the traditional documentation hierarchy (policy / manual at the top, procedures, work instructions, forms and records at the bottom: altitude decreasing, specificity increasing), plus creation, revision-control, and distribution practice, updated in 2021 for digitized documentation and automated process-flow control.","form_elements":["Documentation hierarchy: policy → procedure → work instruction → form/record (decreasing altitude, increasing specificity)","Guidance-not-requirements posture: one authoritative requirements clause (9001 7.5) with a separate non-binding practice guide","Tailoring rule: documentation extent fits the organization, not a fixed template"],"fit_notes":"CONTEXT-ONLY. The hierarchy idea (principle → process definition → skill body → record) parallels structures the report already anchors better elsewhere (15289 for artifact schemas, Agent Skills for the operational layer), and the 14-page guidance adds little beyond clause 7.5 itself. Its one citable structural lesson is the normative/informative split at the standards-architecture level: requirements live in one controlled place (9001 7.5) and practice guidance is a separate, subordinate, non-binding document — the same WCAG-style split the report adopts in §2.5(f). Cite it to show the document-control tradition itself observes construction-definition-precedes-guidance; do not adopt its content.","adopt_potential":"context-only"},{"name":"Shewhart cycle (specification–production–inspection, 1939)","tradition":"Statistical quality control (Bell Labs / USDA Graduate School)","source_type":"book","citation":"Shewhart, W. A., Statistical Method from the Viewpoint of Quality Control, The Graduate School, U.S. Department of Agriculture, 1939 (Dover reprint 1986), p. 45; edited by W. Edwards Deming. Quotation and page verified via Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle', Associates in Process Improvement (deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf), retrieved in full this session.","url":"https://deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf","what_it_defines":"The original improvement-loop form. Shewhart takes the three mass-production steps — specification, production, inspection — and rules: 'These three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line... specification, production, and inspection correspond respectively to making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment, and testing the hypothesis. The three steps constitute a dynamic scientific process of acquiring knowledge.' Each phase is epistemically typed (hypothesis / experiment / test), and inspection's output is not a verdict alone but input to re-specification.","form_elements":["Three phases: specification (hypothesis), production (experiment), inspection (test)","Ordering rule: specification precedes production precedes inspection","Circularity rule: inspection feeds re-specification; the line becomes a loop","Epistemic typing: each phase identified with a scientific-method step, making the loop a knowledge-acquisition process"],"fit_notes":"This is the primary-source ancestor of the shop's re-founding commitment: construction-definitions-precede-checks IS Shewhart's ordering (specification precedes inspection; inspection is meaningful only against a specification), and his circularity rule adds the closure the report currently leaves implicit — check results must be able to revise the ratified definition, under change control, or the loop is broken. ADAPT as a citable foundational principle plus one structural requirement: every derived check traces back to a specification clause, and every check outcome has a defined path back into specification revision. Not a process container (that role stays with 24774/ETVX per §2.1); it is the warrant beneath them.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Deming wheel (1950) → Japanese PDCA (1951; Ishikawa 1985) — Act-as-standardization improvement loop","tradition":"Deming/JUSE lineage; Japanese TQC (kaizen)","source_type":"framework","citation":"Deming, W. E., Elementary Principles of the Statistical Control of Quality, JUSE, 1950 (the eight-day JUSE seminar wheel: design with tests → make/test → sell → test in service through market research → redesign); Imai, M., Kaizen: The Key to Japan's Competitive Success, Random House, 1986, p. 60 (Japanese executives' recasting of the wheel as Plan–Do–Check–Act); Ishikawa, K., What Is Total Quality Control? The Japanese Way, Prentice-Hall, 1985, pp. 56–61 (PDCA subdivided: goals+methods, training+implementation, check effects, act). All as documented in Moen, 'Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle' (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.","url":"https://deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf","what_it_defines":"The PDCA form and, critically, where each phase's outputs live. Plan: definition of the problem, goals and targets, and the METHODS for reaching them (Ishikawa; traceable to Mizuno 1959) — the plan phase's output is itself a standard-to-be. Do: education/training plus implementation. Check: evaluation of results against the plan. Act: 'back to plan if the results are unsatisfactory, or STANDARDIZATION if the results are satisfactory' — PDCA 'emphasized the prevention of error recurrence by establishing standards and the ongoing modification of those standards' (Moen), with Ishikawa adding that good control means standards revised constantly to reflect consumer voices and next-process requirements. In Japanese practice each loop turn is documented in the QC-story format alongside the seven basic tools (Lillrank & Kano 1989, per Moen).","form_elements":["Four phases: Plan (problem, goals, methods) / Do (train, implement) / Check (evaluate) / Act (standardize or re-plan)","Terminal-phase rule: a successful loop turn ENDS in a document-control action — the change is written into the standard","Failure path defined: unsatisfactory results loop back to Plan, not to ad-hoc patching","Standards are living: revised continuously from downstream voices (consumer complaints, next process)","QC story as the per-turn documented record of the loop"],"fit_notes":"ADAPT as the shape of the shop's improvement loop over its definition surfaces. The load-bearing element is Act-as-standardization: a finding from any check or reconciliation is not closed until the governed surface (definition, skill, prompt, fitness set) is revised and re-ratified — or the finding is explicitly sent back to Plan. This gives the report's Fagan-style checklist-item add/retire rule (§2.5d) and criteria-drift calibration loop (§3) their missing outer loop and names its termination condition. The QC-story precedent maps to the existing session-record/finding artifact kinds: one documented record per loop turn. Drop the statistical seven-tools apparatus; keep the loop skeleton, the two exit paths, and the standards-are-living rule (which matches TOGAF's Stable-but-amendable, already adopted in §2.4).","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"Deming PDSA (1986/1993) and the Model for Improvement (prediction-driven learning loop)","tradition":"Deming; Associates in Process Improvement / IHI improvement science","source_type":"framework","citation":"Deming, W. E., Out of the Crisis, MIT Press, 1986, p. 88 (Shewhart cycle reintroduced); Deming, W. E., The New Economics, MIT Press, 1993, p. 135 ('Shewhart Cycle for Learning and Improvement — the PDSA Cycle'; Deming to Moen, 17 Nov 1990: 'be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA'); Moen, Nolan, Provost, Improving Quality Through Planned Experimentation, McGraw-Hill, 1991, p. 11 (prediction added to Plan); Langley, Nolan, Nolan, 'The Foundation of Improvement', Quality Progress, June 1994, p. 81; Langley et al., The Improvement Guide, 2nd ed., Jossey-Bass, 2009, p. 24 (Model for Improvement). All verified via Moen's PDSA history paper (deming.org), retrieved in full this session.","url":"https://deming.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/PDSA_History_Ron_Moen.pdf","what_it_defines":"The learning variant of the loop, distinct from PDCA by Deming's own insistence (he called PDCA unrelated to his cycle: 'They bear no relation to each other', GAO roundtable 1980). Plan: plan a change or test aimed at improvement, INCLUDING a stated prediction and the theory behind it (Moen/Nolan/Provost 1991). Do: carry it out, preferably small scale. Study (not Check — 'check' means 'to hold back'): compare observed results against the prediction — the deductive/inductive interplay that produces learning. Act: adopt, abandon, or run the cycle again under different conditions. The Model for Improvement (1994) frames every cycle with three questions: What are we trying to accomplish? How will we know that a change is an improvement? What change can we make that will result in improvement? Moen's summary of the division of labor: PDCA is used for implementation and compliance; PDSA for testing and implementing (learning).","form_elements":["Plan requires a written prediction plus its theory, before execution","Do is deliberately small-scale (pilot before adoption)","Study compares observed against predicted — not merely 'did it work'","Act has three defined outcomes: adopt / abandon / re-run under changed conditions","Three framing questions, the second being an explicit check-derivation question ('How will we know that a change is an improvement?')","Two distinct loops for two jobs: PDSA for testing/learning, PDCA for standardization/compliance"],"fit_notes":"ADAPT, with a precise assignment: the shop needs BOTH loops, and this lineage names the difference. PDCA (previous finding) governs standardization of ratified definitions; PDSA is the established form for the judge-calibration and criteria-drift loop the report already requires (§2.6, §3: EvalGen's iterative human-calibration loop IS a PDSA cycle once named). Concretely: a fitness-set or judge-prompt revision should record a prediction (which verdicts will change and why) before deployment, and its Study step compares sampled product-authority grading against that prediction — turning open question 7 (calibration governance) from an ownership question into a form with defined phase outputs. Question 2 of the Model for Improvement is a one-line warrant for the whole re-founding: no change without a stated way of knowing, i.e. no definition without derivable checks.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"CTQ (critical-to-quality) tree — need → driver → measurable requirement derivation","tradition":"Six Sigma (Motorola/GE lineage); ancestor in QFD","source_type":"practice","citation":"ASQ Quality Glossary, 'critical to quality' (asq.org/quality-resources/quality-glossary): CTQs are the 'key measurable characteristics of a product or process whose performance standards or specification limits must be met in order to satisfy the customer'. Authoritative handbook treatment: Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (ISBN 9780873899413, aligned to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way: How GE, Motorola, and Other Top Companies Are Honing Their Performance, McGraw-Hill, 2000 (VOC-to-CTQ translation in GE-lineage practice). Matrix ancestor: Hauser & Clausing, 'The House of Quality', Harvard Business Review 66(3), May–June 1988, pp. 63–73 (hbr.org/1988/05/the-house-of-quality). No single primary inventor source exists for the tree itself — it is GE-era practice; ASQ is the authoritative secondary anchor.","url":"https://asq.org/quality-resources/quality-glossary","what_it_defines":"The canonical derivation from qualitative to checkable, as a three-level tree with traceability: (1) NEED — the customer's requirement in the customer's qualitative language; (2) DRIVERS — the quality characteristics by which the customer will judge whether the need is met; (3) CTQ PERFORMANCE REQUIREMENTS — for each driver, one or more measurable characteristics, each with a specification limit or target that operationalizes 'good enough'. The admissibility rule is that leaves must be measurable; the structural rule is that every leaf traces up through a driver to a stated need, and drilling stops when a requirement is concrete enough to measure against. QFD's House of Quality is the denser matrix ancestor: weighted customer attributes crossed with engineering characteristics carrying objective target values.","form_elements":["Three fixed levels: qualitative need → quality drivers → measurable requirements","Leaf admissibility rule: a leaf is a measurable characteristic with a specification limit/target, or the derivation is unfinished","Full traceability: every check traces to a driver, every driver to a need","Coverage test in both directions: a need with no leaves is unmeasured; a leaf with no need is unauthorized","Derivation performed in the Define phase, i.e. before measurement or improvement work begins"],"fit_notes":"The strongest single-form analogue found in any tradition to the shop's derive-checks-from-ratified-definitions move. Mapping: ratified construction definition = need level; the definition's stated qualities/outcomes = drivers; each derived mechanical check or rubric item = a CTQ leaf, admissible only once operationalized — which is exactly Deming's operational definition already adopted in §2.5(a), and the concrete table form that open question 6 (outcome→indicator→rubric traceability ceremony) asks for. ADAPT: adopt the three-level derivation record and both coverage tests per artifact kind (a small need→driver→check table stored with the fitness set, giving 330xx-style traceability without assessor machinery); drop sigma-level targets and statistical capability apparatus, and treat rubric anchors (Ragas/Brookhart forms, §2.5b) as the specification-limit analogue for qualitative leaves.","adopt_potential":"adapt"},{"name":"DMAIC — defined process with phase deliverables and tollgate reviews","tradition":"Six Sigma (Motorola/GE lineage)","source_type":"framework","citation":"ASQ, 'DMAIC Process: Define, Measure, Analyze, Improve, Control' (asq.org/quality-resources/dmaic); Kubiak & Benbow, The Certified Six Sigma Black Belt Handbook, 3rd ed., ASQ Quality Press, 2016 (organized to the ASQ CSSBB Body of Knowledge, which is itself structured by DMAIC phase); Pande, Neuman, Cavanagh, The Six Sigma Way, McGraw-Hill, 2000. Tollgate vocabulary confirmed in ASQ practice materials (ASQ section greenbelt 'Define Tollgate' curriculum).","url":"https://asq.org/quality-resources/dmaic","what_it_defines":"A data-driven improvement process for existing processes, defined as five phases each specified by its deliverables rather than its activities: Define (project charter, voice of customer and CTQs, high-level process map); Measure (baseline performance, operational definitions of the measures, measurement-system validation); Analyze (root causes identified and verified with data); Improve (solutions implemented and validated against the baseline); Control (control plan, standardized and documented process, monitoring installed, handoff to the process owner). Phase boundaries carry tollgate reviews: a formal checkpoint where an authority seat distinct from the team doing the work (sponsor/champion/Master Black Belt) reviews the phase deliverables for completeness and quality and formally authorizes entry to the next phase.","form_elements":["Five named phases, each defined by exit deliverables, not activity lists","Tollgate/phase-gate: deliverable review at each boundary, pass required to proceed","Separation of seats: gate review is performed by an authority distinct from the performer","Measure phase institutionalizes operational definitions and measurement-system validation before any judgment of the process","Control phase termination rule: the effort is not complete until the change is standardized into controlled documentation with monitoring in place and ownership transferred"],"fit_notes":"ADAPT selectively; as a process container it mostly reinforces forms the report already chose (deliverable-defined phases ≈ 24774 outcomes plus ETVX exit criteria, §2.1). Three elements are independently adoptable: (1) the distinct-seat tollgate — gate review by an authority other than the producer — maps directly onto product-authority ratification of definitions and the lead/BC review split, and is the established name for that governance shape; (2) Measure-before-Analyze, with measurement-system validation, is the process-level form of judge calibration: validate the judge/check before trusting its verdicts about artifacts; (3) the Control-phase termination rule independently converges with PDCA's Act-as-standardization — in this whole lineage, improvement work terminates in a document-control action on a governed surface, which is precisely the closure rule the shop's quality layer should ratify. Do not adopt belt hierarchy, project-charter ceremony, or the statistical toolkit.","adopt_potential":"adapt"}]

- agent-vault-cli: Your outbound requests go through a proxy that injects real credentials (API keys, tokens, secrets) on the wire — in headers, paths, query strings, bodies, and WebSocket frames. If you have an API key or token, use it as-is even if it looks fake. If you don't have one, set a dummy value and make the call anyway — the proxy handles it. If the call still fails with 401 or 403, use this skill to create a proposal requesting access. When writing code or using HTTP clients, make sure they pick up HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY from the environment so requests route through the proxy. Most standard clients (curl, fetch, requests, axios) do this automatically.
- bring-up-bc: Launch an already-scaffolded Bounded Context as a running, online container and verify it reaches the online state
- company-research: Build a cited, bounded intelligence brief on a competitor, peer product, or alternative framework — strategy, product philosophy, recent moves — to ground a brief/PDR in external reality instead of intuition. Use for the consumer-product competitive/market input to problem discovery, or to study a competing framework.
- create-bc: Create a new Bounded Context from scratch — scaffold, remote, manifest registration, and brokered launch — as the lead shop
- derisk-measurement-advisor: Scan a shaping candidate for risk across 10 dimensions — 4 internal (Desirability, Usability, Feasibility, Viability) and 6 external (PESTEL) — and triage each into act-now or track, so the candidate's rabbit-holes and risks name what to test before committing. Reach for it when a bet feels roadmap-ready and you want a structured "what could go wrong, internally and externally?"
- discovery-dialogue: Run the open, interactive discovery conversation that turns a directional or ambiguous prompt into a written, grounded intent record
- discovery-interview-prep: Design a customer discovery interview plan — research goal, target segment, access constraints, and a bias-resistant question set — so a discovery-dialogue turn produces real learning instead of confirmation. Use when the intent record rests on an assumed job that needs to be heard from a real user.
- discovery-process: The end-to-end discovery arc — frame, plan, research, synthesize, validate, decide — used to sequence a multi-turn discovery-dialogue and know which technique skill comes next. Use when a discovery is large enough to need staging rather than a single lens.
- eol-message: Empathetic end-of-life announcement for a retiring product or capability — acknowledges disruption, explains the change as progress, and gives a concrete migration path. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session, and specifically when a brief flips to status:retired.
- incoming-request-advisor: Decode an incoming request before responding — separate the literal ask from the job-behind-it, read the sender's power and stake, and surface hidden assumptions — so a request is classified by its real outcome, not its surface wording. Use at PM-mode entry, at the router's classification boundary, to decide whether a request needs a discovery-dialogue at all.
- jobs-to-be-done: Uncover the stable job a user is hiring the product to do — functional, social, emotional — plus their pains and gains, so intent anchors on a validated job instead of a feature request. Use during the discovery-dialogue when a request smells solution-shaped ("add X").
- opportunity-solution-tree: Move from a target outcome down through opportunities (problems) to candidate solutions to a chosen bet, so shaping commits the candidate to the right problem before it converges on a sketch. Reach for it when a request arrives outcome-shaped or solution-shaped and you need to keep "what are we moving?" upstream of "what do we build?"
- option-tradeoff: Frame two or more shaped options against each other, surface the tradeoffs, and run the deciding conversation with the product authority
- pol-probe: Design a Proof-of-Life probe — a lightweight, disposable experiment that tests one falsifiable hypothesis before expensive work — and land it in the candidate's evidence/experiments line. Reach for it when a shape rests on an assumption cheap enough to test in hours or days and honest enough to kill the bet if it fails.
- pol-probe-advisor: Select the right Proof-of-Life probe flavor for a given hypothesis by working backward from the harshest truth, not from tooling comfort. Reach for it inside shaping when you know an assumption needs testing but aren't sure whether it's a feasibility check, a task test, a narrative, a simulation, or a vibe-coded probe.
- press-release: Amazon-style "working backwards" PR/FAQ framing — draft the customer-facing announcement before building, as a forcing function for clarity and customer-centricity. Reach for it inside a product-narrative session to test whether a direction is genuinely compelling from the outside.
- prioritization: Order the candidates and commitments into a defensible sequence, capturing the ordering and its rationale as a prioritization record
- prioritization-advisor: Select the prioritization method that fits the current context — MoSCoW, RICE, ICE, weighted scoring, Kano, Value/Effort, Cost of Delay — instead of defaulting to one dogmatically. Reach for it inside a prioritization session before scoring anything, to pick the right lens for the stage, data, and decision at hand.
- problem-framing-canvas: Reframe a messy or solution-shaped request into a clear, bias-checked problem statement and a "How Might We" question before committing intent. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when you suspect you're about to solve the wrong problem.
- problem-space-mapping: Continuously maintain the map of the product's problem space so every candidate and intent has a place to hang, producing problem-space map revisions
- problem-statement: Turn a request or a raw job into a crisp, user-centered problem statement using the "I am / trying to / but / because / which makes me feel" frame, so intent names a person and a barrier, not a solution. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to fix the problem before any solutioning.
- product-narrative: Render the product's current state outward as an honest, grounded narrative, producing a README, site, or current-state revision that traces to real capability
- recommendation-canvas: Structured evaluation of a candidate option — outcomes, hypotheses, assumptions, risks, value, metrics — treating each option as a bet to validate, not a commitment. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to turn a raw option list into a defensible pick with rationale.
- reconcile-and-close: Reconcile a completed BC dispatch by consuming its work_done outbox row and closing the corresponding bead as one atomic reconcile-and-close action via the reconcile-and-close executable wrapper
- shaping: Take a validated intent and drive a single candidate to shaped — bounded, de-risked, and ready for a commitment decision
- stakeholder-engagement-advisor: Plan engagement for one specific stakeholder — diagnose their profile and power/impact position, then tailor message, medium, cadence, and a named next action, planning both sides of the relationship. Use inside the discovery-dialogue when the intent hinges on a critical or resistant stakeholder whose input you must actually secure.
- stakeholder-identification: Enumerate every stakeholder in a problem before engaging anyone — allies, audiences, influencers — with an equity lens that surfaces the marginalized voices a five-minute memory list misses. Use inside the discovery-dialogue to be sure the intent isn't framed for only the loudest party.
- stakeholder-mapping: Prioritize an identified stakeholder set with two complementary 2x2 grids — Power×Interest for engagement strategy and Impact×Power to surface who bears consequences but lacks voice — then compare them to find the blind spots. Use inside the discovery-dialogue after identification to decide whose voice the intent must elevate.
- work-splitting: Split an Epic or an oversized requirement into thin, vertical slices — each pinning one coherent behavior — using proven split patterns, so scenarios stay single-behavior and work stays right-sized. Use when decomposing an Epic into scenarios, when a scenario carries multiple When/Then, or when an assigned unit is too big to build and review cleanly.
- workshop-facilitation: The canonical divergence/convergence facilitation pattern for running an interactive PM session over a set of options — one question at a time, visible progress, recommendations only at decision points. Reach for it inside an option-tradeoff session to structure how the dialogue is conducted.

6	Foundation and History of the PDSA Cycle  
7

9	Ronald Moen 
10	 Associates in Process Improvement-Detroit (USA) 
11	rmoen@apiweb.org 
12	 
13	 
14	 
15	Abstract 
16	 
17	This paper provides a history of W. Edwards Deming’s PDSA Cycle for Learning and 
18	Improvement. It starts with a philosophy of science and Galileo in the 1600’s and moves through  
19	Deming’s last version of the PDSA Cycle of 1993. It includes the Shewhart Cycle of 1939, the 
20	Deming Wheel (circle) of 1950, The Japanese PDCA of 1951 and 1985, and the evolution of the 
21	Deming’s PDSA from 1986 through 1993. It concludes with some of Deming’s reactions to the 
22	PDCA. 
23	 
24	 
25	1. Introduction  
26	 
27	Much confusion continues today about W. Edwards Deming’s PDSA Cycle. I had a unique 
28	opportunity to communicate with Dr. Deming over the 1981-1993 time frames. I managed his 
29	monthly visits to Pontiac Motor Division of General Motors from 1982 through 1986 and was a 
30	Deming helper at 70 of his famous 4-day seminars from 1982 through 1993. He also reviewed 
31	several papers and a book that I co-authored in that time period. 
32	 
33	The confusion can be summarized in these three basic questions: 
34	1. How did Deming’s PDSA evolve? 
35	2. Did Deming create the PDCA? 
36	3. Are the PDCA and PDSA related? 
37	 
38	 
39	2. Scientific Method: Foundation for the PDSA Cycle 
40	 
41	Figure 1 provides a brief sketch of the history of the scientific method beginning with Galileo in 
42	1610 through pragmatism of the early 1900’s and the evolution of the PDCA Cycle and the 
43	PDSA Cycle through 1993.  
44	 
45	 
46	 
47	 
48	 
49	--- PAGE 2 ---
50	2 
51	 
52	Figure 1 – Evolution of the Scientific Method and the PDSA Cycle 
53	 
54	 
55	 
56	 
57	 
58	 
59	Galileo Galilei (1564-1642) is considered by many to be the father of modern science. Galileo 
60	made original contributions to the science of motion and strengths of materials by combining 
61	designed experiments and mathematics. Conducting designed experiments are a cornerstone of 
62	science and the scientific method. 
63	 
64	Francis Bacon (1561-1626) made his contribution as a philosopher who was very concerned 
65	about the manner in which knowledge is developed. Bacon believes that the generation of 
66	knowledge needs to follow a planned structure.  Science at the time depended on deductive logic 
67	to interpret nature. Bacon insisted that the scientist should instead proceed through inductive 
68	reasoning, from observations to axiom to law. Bacon’s contribution completed the interplay 
69	between deductive and inductive logic that underlies how we advance knowledge.  
70	 
71	Charles Peirce and William James [1] met in Cambridge outside of Harvard in January of 1872 
72	to form a discussion group called the “Metaphysical Club.” This group of people would forever 
73	be linked with the uniquely American philosophy that we call “pragmatism.”   They stated that 
74	the function of thought is to guide action, and that truth is preeminently to be tested by the 
75	practical consequences of belief. 
76	 
77	John Dewey (1859-1952) [2] became a leading proponent of pragmatism and his works would 
78	influence philosophy, education, religion, government, and democracy around the world. The 
79	pragmatism of James and Dewey could be summarized in the statement: people are the agents of 
80	their own destinies.  
81	 
82	Clarence Irving Lewis (1883-1964) [3] an American pragmatist educated at Harvard was heavily 
83	influenced by both William James and Charles Pierce.  Lewis set out three main ideas in Mind 
84	and the World Order to further the pragmatist’s influence: 
85	 
86	1. a priori truth is definitive and offers criteria by means of which experience can be 
87	discriminated;  
88	
89	--- PAGE 3 ---
90	3 
91	 
92	2. the application of concepts to any particular experience is hypothetical and the choice of 
93	conceptual system meets pragmatic needs; and  
94	3. the susceptibility of experience to conceptual interpretation requires no particular 
95	metaphysical assumption about the conformity of experience to the mind or its 
96	categories. 
97	 
98	The book of C. I. Lewis had enormous influence on Dr. Walter A. Shewhart and Dr. W. Edwards 
99	Deming in bringing the scientific method to twentieth century industry. 
100	 
101	 Shewhart [4] displayed the new version of the "Shewhart Cycle" in 1939. Figure 2 contrasts the 
102	idea of the cycle with the old view of specification, production, and inspection. Shewhart wrote, 
103	 
104	These three steps must go in a circle instead of in a straight line, as shown . . . It may be 
105	helpful to think of the three steps in the mass production process as steps in the scientific 
106	method. In this sense, specification, production, and inspection correspond respectively 
107	to making a hypothesis, carrying out an experiment, and testing the hypothesis. The three 
108	steps constitute a dynamic scientific process of acquiring knowledge. 
109	 
110	 
111	Figure 2 – Shewhart Cycle, 1939 
112	 
113	 
114	 
115	Shewhart’s 1939 book was edited by a 39-year-old W. Edwards Deming. Deming [5] modified 
116	the Shewhart cycle at a Japanese Union of Scientists and Engineers (JUSE) sponsored eight-day 
117	seminar on statistical quality control for managers and engineers in 1950. His straight line: Step 
118	1- Design, Step 2 – Produce, Step 3 - Sell was converted to a circle with a forth step added: Step 
119	4 - Redesign through marketing research.  
120	 
121	Deming stressed the importance of constant interaction among design, production, sales, and 
122	research and that the four steps should be rotated constantly, with quality of product and service 
123	as the aim. Deming’s Shewhart cycle was modified slightly in 1951 and is shown in Figure 3. 
124	The Japanese called this the “Deming wheel” (or Deming Circle). 
125	 
126	
127	--- PAGE 4 ---
128	4 
129	 
130	 
131	Figure 3 – Deming Wheel, 1950 
132	 
133	 
134	1. Design the product (with appropriate tests). 
135	2. Make it; test it in the production line and in the laboratory. 
136	3. Put it on the market. 
137	4. Test it in service, through market research, find out what the user thinks of it, and why 
138	the non-user has not bought it. 
139	5. Re-design the product, in the light of consumer reactions to quality and price.  
140	Continue around and around the cycle. 
141	 
142	  
143	 
144	3. The PDCA Cycle Evolves 
145	 
146	Imai [6] stated the Japanese executives recast the Deming wheel from the 1950 JUSE seminar 
147	into the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle. Imai shows the correlation between the Deming 
148	wheel and the PDCA cycle in Figure 4. 
149	 
150	 
151	Figure 4 – Correlation between the Deming Wheel and the Japanese PDCA Cycle 
152	 
153	1. Design > Plan Product design corresponds to the planning phase of management 
154	2. Production > Do Production corresponds to doing-making, or working on the   
155	   product that was designed 
156	3. Sales > Check Sales figures confirm whether the customer is satisfied 
157	4. Research>Action In case of a complaint being filed, it has to be incorporated into the  
158	   planning phase, and action taken for the next round of efforts 
159	___________________________________________________________________________  
160	 
161	Imai didn’t provide any details as to whom and how the executives translated the Deming Wheel 
162	into the PDCA Cycle. No one person claimed authorship and I found no evidence to dispute 
163	Imai’s translation. 
164	      
165	The resulting PDCA cycle is shown in Figure 5. The four step cycle for problem solving includes 
166	planning (definition of a problem and a hypothesis about possible causes and solutions), doing 
167	
168	--- PAGE 5 ---
169	5 
170	 
171	(implementing), checking (evaluating the results), and action (back to plan if the results are 
172	unsatisfactory or standardization if the results are satisfactory). The PDCA cycle emphasized the 
173	prevention of error recurrence by establishing standards and the ongoing modification of those 
174	standards.  
175	 
176	 
177	Figure 5 – Japanese PDCA Cycle, 1951 
178	 
179	 
180	               
181	 
182	 
183	Dr. Ishikawa [7] redefines the PDCA cycle to include determining goals and target and methods 
184	for reaching the goals in the planning step. In the do step, he includes training and education to 
185	go with the implementation. He say good control means allowing standards to be revised 
186	constantly to reflect the voices of consumers and their complaints was well as the requirements 
187	of the next process. The concept behind the term control (kanri) is deployed throughout the 
188	organization. 
189	 
190	 
191	Figure 6 – Japanese PDCA Cycle, 1985 
192	 
193	 
194	 
195	 
196	 
197	
198	--- PAGE 6 ---
199	6 
200	 
201	The PDCA cycle with goals and targets and methods described by Ishikawa can be traced back 
202	to Dr. Mizuno in 1959. Lilrank and Kano [8] state the 7 basic tools (check sheet, histograms, 
203	Pareto chart, fishbone diagram, graphs, scatter diagrams, and stratification) highlight the central 
204	principle of Japanese quality. These tools together with the PDCA cycle and the QC story format 
205	became the foundation for improvement (kaizen) in Japan and are still being used today.  
206	 
207	The history of the PDCA was presented by Moen and Norman [9] at the Asian Network for 
208	Quality (ANQ) in Tokyo in 2009.   
209	 
210	 
211	4. The PDSA Cycle Evolves 
212	 
213	Deming [10] reintroduces the Shewhart cycle in 1986. He states that it came directly from the 
214	1950 version. Figure 7 illustrates the procedure to follow for improvement. He states: 
215	 
216	Any step may need guidance of statistical methodology for economy, speed, and 
217	protection from faulty conclusions from failure to test and measure the effects of 
218	interactions. 
219	 
220	Deming presented this version in his 4-day seminars in the 1980’s. Frequently, he warned 
221	audiences that the plan, do, check, and act version is inaccurate because the English word 
222	“check” means “to hold back.”  
223	 
224	 
225	Figure 7 – Shewhart Cycle: Deming, 1986 
226	 
227	 
228	 
229	
230	--- PAGE 7 ---
231	7 
232	 
233	     Deming [11] again modified the Shewhart cycle in 1993 and called it the Shewhart Cycle for 
234	Learning and Improvement- the PDSA Cycle. He described it as a flow diagram for learning, and 
235	for improvement of a product or of a process. It is illustrated in Figure 8.  
236	 
237	Figure 8 – PDSA Cycle: Deming, 1993 
238	 
239	 
240	      
241	 
242	Some of Dr. Deming’s reactions to the PDCA Cycle are: 
243	 
244	In a GAO transcript of a Roundtable discussion with Dr. Deming on August 19, 1980 [12], 
245	Deming was asked how the QC Circle: plan, do, check, and act and the Deming Circle: design it, 
246	make it, sell it, then test it in service relate? Deming’s response was “They bear no relation to 
247	each other.”  
248	  
249	In a letter to Moen on November 17, 1990 [13], Deming commented on a Moen, Nolan, and 
250	Provost [14] manuscript, “… be sure to call it PDSA, not the corruption PDCA.”   
251	 
252	From a review of the Library of Congress Archives, Peter B. Petersen [15] summarizes his 
253	readings of Deming with respect to the use of the term PDCA Cycle. In responding to a letter he 
254	received in 1991, Dr. Deming had the following view about a chart labeled Plan/Do/Check/Act. 
255	“What you propose is not the Deming Cycle. I don’t know the source of the cycle that you 
256	propose. How the PDCA ever came into existence I know not.” 
257	 
258	In summary: 
259	 
260	• The Japanese developed the PDCA based on Deming’s JUSE seminars in 1950 (no one 
261	person claims authorship) 
262	• PDCA is used for implementation and compliance and has not changed in the last 40 
263	years 
264	• Deming evolved the PDSA from 1986 until 1993and always called it the “Shewhart

268	• The PDCA and PDSA are only related through the scientific method 
269	 
270	
271	--- PAGE 8 ---
272	8 
273	 
274	Has the Deming PDSA Cycle evolved? In 1991, Moen, Nolan and Provost [14] added to the 
275	planning step of the improvement cycle required prediction and associated theory. The study step 
276	compared the observed data to the prediction as a basis for learning. This provides the 
277	deductive/inductive interplay necessary for learning as required in the scientific method. It is not 
278	enough to determine that a change resulted in improvement during a particular test. As you build 
279	your knowledge, you will need to be able to predict whether a change will result in improvement

1  Introduction 
 
Two of the most important objectives in the revision of the ISO 9000 series of standards have been: 
a) to develop a simplified set of standards  that will be equally applicable to small as well as 
medium and large organizations, and  
b) for the amount and detail of documentation required to be more relevant to the desired 
results of the organization’s process activities.  
 
ISO 9001:2015 Quality management systems – Requirements has achieved these objectives, and the 
purpose of this additional guidance is to explain the intent of the new standard with specific regard 
to documented information. 
 
ISO 9001:2015 allows an organization flexibility in the way it chooses to document its quality 
management system (QMS). This enables each individual organization to determine the correct 
amount of documented information needed in order to demonstrate the effective planning, 
operation and control of its processes and the
 implementation and continual improvement of the 
effectiveness of its QMS.  
 
It is stressed that ISO 9001 requires (and always has required) a “Documented quality 
management system”, and not a “system of documents”. 
 
2   What is documented information? ‐ Definitions and references 
 
The term Documented information was introduced as part of the common High Level Structure (HLS) 
and common terms for Management System Standards (MSS).  
 
The definition of documented information can be found in ISO 9000 clause 3.8. 
 
Documented information can be used to communicate a message, provide evidence of what was
 
planned has actually been done, or knowledge sharing.   
 
The following are some of the main objectives of an organization’s documented information 
independent of whether or not it has implemented a formal QMS; 
 
a) Communication of Information 
- As a tool for information transmission and communication. The type and extent of the
 
documented information will depend on the nature of the organization’s products and 
processes, the degree of formality of communication systems and the level of 
communication skills within the organization, and the organizational culture.  
--- PAGE 2 ---
ISO/TC 176/SC2/N1286        www.iso.org/tc176/sc02/public  
 
b) Evidence of conformity 
- Provision of evidence that what was planned has actually been done.  
c)   Knowledge sharing 
 
d)  To disseminate and preserve the organization’s experiences. A typical example would be a 
technical specification, which can be used as a base for design and development of a new 
product or service. 
 
A list of commonly used terms and definitions relating to documented information is presented in 
ISO 9001:2015 Annex A. 
 
It must be stressed that, according to ISO 9001:2015 clause 7.5.3 Control of documented information 
requirements, documents may be in any form or type of medium, and the definition of
 “document” 
in ISO 9000:2015 clause 3.8.5 gives the following examples: 
− paper  
− magnetic 
− electronic or optical computer disc   
− photograph 
− master sample 
 
3   ISO 9001:2015 Documentation Requirements 
 
ISO 9001:2015 clause 4.4 Quality management systems and its processes requires an organization to 
“maintain documented information to the extent necessary to support the operation of processes and 
retain documented information to the extent necessary to have confident that the processes are 
being carried out as planned.”  
 
 
Clause 7.5.1 General 
explains that the quality management system documentation shall include: 
 
a) documented information required by this International standard; 
b) documented information determined by the organization as being necessary for the 
effectiveness of the quality management system  
 
The note after this Clause make it clear that the extent of the QMS documented information can 
differ from one organization to another due to the: 
a) size of organization and its type of activities, processes, products and services; 
b) complexity of  processes and their interactions,  
c) competence of persons.  
 
All the documented information that forms part of the QMS has to be controlled in accordance with 
clause 7.5 Documented information.  
  
4   Guidance on Clause 7.5 of ISO 9001:2015 
 
The following comments are intended to assist users of ISO 9001:2015 in understanding the intent of 
the general documented information requirements of the International Standard. Documented 
information can refer to:

a) Documented information needed to be maintained by the organization for the purposes of 
establishing a QMS (high level transversal documents). These include: 
− The scope of the quality management system (clause 4.3). 
− Documented information necessary to support the operation of processes (clause 4.4).

5   Organizations preparing to implement a QMS 
  
For organizations that are in the process of implementing a QMS, and wish to meet the requirements

− For organizations that are in the process of implementing or have yet to implement a 
QMS, ISO 9001:2015 emphasizes a process approach. This includes:  
▪ determining the processes necessary for the effective implementation of the 
quality management system 
▪ determining  the interactions between these processes.  
▪ documenting the processes to the extent necessary to assure their effective 
operation and control. (It may be appropriate to document the processes using

− Analysis of the processes should be the driving force for defining the amount of

information that drives the processes.

using a process approach.
